newsitem.title: FRANCE: Slow French growth shows task for finance minister.
newsitem.headline: Slow French growth shows task for finance minister.

text.p: France's new Socialist finance minister took office on Thursday with the unenviable task of getting public finances into shape for European monetary union after promising to spare voters further economic austerity.

Dominique Strauss-Kahn took over a newly merged finance and industry portfolio the same day as the INSEE statistics office released data showing economic growth made a relatively lacklustre start in the first quarter of 1997.
The 48-year-old finance and industry minister inherits an economy in the test year for joining a single European currency.

Some economists say data showing a 0.2 percent rise in gross domestic product for the first three months of 1997 augurs badly for the full year, although most financial markets have long been predicting that a pick-up would in any case be tilted towards the second half of this year.
Ministers were still fine-tuning their responsibilities after the left-wing government was named on Wednesday evening by Prime Minister Lionel Jospin.
But Strauss-Kahn, the principal author of Socialist Party economic policy, will clearly have his hands full.
There was already considerable speculation about the ability of the previous centre-right government to meet its objectives on public deficit control.

Strauss-Kahn has the additional task of reconciling deficit control requirements which go hand-in-hand with a commitment to join monetary union in 1999 with an election pledge to promote growth and jobs and avoid further public spending cutbacks.

The centre-right government ousted in Sunday's parliamentary election had forecast economic growth of a minimum 2.3 percent in 1997 and said it would limit the public deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) to qualify for monetary union.

The Socialists, who dominate the new coalition, have accused their predecessors of choking consumer spending, and growth as a result, by hiking value-added tax and slamming the brakes too hard on public spending.
What could prove crucial for Strauss-Kahn, along with his new budget minister colleague, is an audit of state finances called for by Jospin. No date has yet been set for that reassessment.

Strauss-Kahn and Jospin will have to work out whether the public deficit can be limited this year to three percent of GDP and, if not, what kind of overshoot they can live with and defend in front of their European partners.

During the election campaign, they made it clear they backed a single currency launch on time in 1999 but said people should not be subjected to further austerity based on a rigid, arithmetical view that the public deficit had to be cut to precisely 3.0 percent of GDP to qualify.

The pressure on state finances could mount significantly, however, if the Socialist-led coalition finds itself confronted with demands for a hefty rise in pay for several million civil servants and a big hike in the national minimum wage.

Trade unions universally opposed the previous government's decision to impose a 2.8 percent pay increase spread over this year and next and are expected to renew their demands for at least a "catch-up payment" after a pay freeze in 1996.

In the background to all of this, prospects for increased economic growth remain cloudy. The data on Thursday showed that business investment fell 1.3 percent in the first quarter of the year, while household spending rose 0.4 percent.
While some analysts felt the first quarter was likely to be the last of several quarters to show weak growth, scepticism about the outlook is still predominant.

"I honestly don't see anything in the figures to think growth will exceed two percent this year," said Joanne Perez, a strategist at Merrill Lynch. "The window of opportunity (for the Socialists) is quite short."
